column1: # subject|title|intuition|deep explanation|formula/reference|fully worked miniature example|speed trick|common trap

PS|Sets and sample spaces|An experiment can produce several outcomes; the sample space contains every possible outcome.|An event is a subset of the sample space. List atomic outcomes first, then group them into events. For equally likely outcomes probability is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.|P(A)=number in A / number in Ω (only equally likely outcomes)|Two fair dice have 36 ordered outcomes. Sum 7 occurs in 6 pairs, so P(sum=7)=6/36=1/6.|Check whether outcomes are equally likely before counting.|Confusing (1,2) and (2,1) when dice are distinguishable.

PS|Counting: addition and multiplication rules|Use addition for mutually exclusive choices and multiplication for sequential choices.|If you can choose a red item in m ways OR a blue item in n ways, add. If a code needs a letter AND digit, multiply. Overlapping alternatives need inclusion-exclusion.|AND -> multiply; disjoint OR -> add|Three shirt choices and four trouser choices give 3×4=12 outfits.|Draw decision slots to avoid missing restrictions.|Adding counts for stages that happen together.

PS|Permutations and arrangements|Order matters when assigning positions.|Arrange r distinct objects selected from n distinct objects without replacement. For circular arrangements of n distinct people, fixing one person removes rotational duplication.|nPr=n!/(n-r)!; circle=(n-1)!|Arrange 3 of 5 students in a row: 5×4×3=60.|If positions are labelled, think permutation first.|Using combinations when seats are distinct.

PS|Combinations and selections|A combination picks a group without caring about the order.|Selections divide permutations by r! because every selected group appears in r! internal orders. Use complement for at least one questions.|nCr=n!/[r!(n-r)!]|Choose 2 of 5 students: 5×4/2=10.|nCr=nC(n-r); count the excluded group if smaller.|Treating AB and BA as different groups.

PS|Probability axioms and complements|Probability is nonnegative, the full space has probability one, and disjoint events add.|The complement contains outcomes not in A; union and intersection obey inclusion-exclusion. These identities do not require equal likelihood.|P(Aᶜ)=1-P(A); P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B)|If P(A)=0.37, then P(not A)=0.63.|For at least one, compute 1-P(none).|Adding overlapping events without subtracting their intersection.

PS|Independent versus disjoint events|Independent means learning A does not change B; disjoint means they cannot happen together.|For independent events the intersection probability factors. If A and B have positive probability and are disjoint, they cannot be independent.|Independent: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B); disjoint: P(A∩B)=0|If P(A)=0.4 and P(B)=0.5 independently, P(both)=0.2.|Ask whether the event can happen together before choosing a rule.|Thinking mutually exclusive implies independent.

PS|Conditional probability|A condition restricts the sample space to cases where B happened.|The denominator is the probability of the condition; it is not always the number of all outcomes. A useful tool for cards, tests and filters.|P(A given B)=P(A∩B)/P(B)|Of 20 people, 8 are engineers and 5 engineers use Python; P(Python given engineer)=5/8.|Read the phrase after 'given' as the denominator population.|Swapping P(A given B) and P(B given A).

PS|Total probability and partition|Break an event into nonoverlapping cases that cover the full population.|Condition on cases B1...Bk and sum each conditional contribution; often pairs with Bayes' theorem.|P(A)=Σ P(A given Bi)P(Bi)|60% from factory 1 with defect 1%, 40% from factory 2 with defect 3%: overall defect=.6(.01)+.4(.03)=.018.|Draw a probability tree; multiply along each branch and add leaves.|Forgetting the base rates of groups.

PS|Bayes theorem|Bayes reverses a conditional probability using prior probabilities.|Update belief after seeing evidence. The denominator is the overall probability of the observed evidence, including false positives.|P(B given A)=P(A given B)P(B)/P(A)|Disease prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive 10%: P(disease given positive)=.009/(.009+.099)=.0833.|Use a hypothetical population of 10,000 to avoid fraction mistakes.|Mistaking test accuracy for posterior probability.

PS|Joint and marginal distributions|Joint distributions describe two variables together; marginals forget one variable.|Sum discrete joint probabilities across one coordinate or integrate a continuous joint density. Conditional distributions divide the joint by the marginal.|P(X=x)=Σy P(X=x,Y=y)|If joint masses at (0,0),(0,1) are .2,.3, P(X=0)=.5.|In a table, marginal totals are row or column sums.|Using the full joint table as the conditional distribution.

PS|Random variables and CDF|A random variable maps outcomes to numbers, not necessarily different numbers.|The cumulative distribution function F(x)=P(X≤x) is nondecreasing, right-continuous, approaches 0 and 1 at extremes. Jumps represent point masses.|F(x)=P(X≤x); P(a<X≤b)=F(b)-F(a)|If X is fair die, F(3)=3/6=.5.|For an interval, subtract CDF endpoints and inspect strict inequalities.|Assuming every CDF is smooth.

PS|Discrete PMF and expectation|A PMF gives the probability at each discrete value; expectation is a probability-weighted average.|The PMF is nonnegative and sums to one. Apply functions inside the sum: E[g(X)] is not usually g(E[X]).|E[X]=Σx x p(x); Σp(x)=1|P(X=0)=.25, P(X=2)=.75: E[X]=1.5.|Check that all masses sum to one before calculating.|Treating an expected value as an outcome that must occur.

PS|Variance and standard deviation|Variance measures squared spread from the mean; standard deviation restores original units.|Variance can be calculated efficiently via second moment minus squared mean. Shifts do not affect variance but scaling by a multiplies it by a².|Var(X)=E[X²]-(E[X])²; Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X)|For fair {0,2}, E[X]=1, E[X²]=2, Var=1.|Second-moment formula is faster than expanding every deviation.|Using a rather than a² for variance under scaling.

PS|Descriptive statistics: mean, median and mode|Mean balances all observations, median is the ordered middle value, and mode is the most frequent value.|For n numbers the mean divides their sum by n. Median is the midpoint for odd n or average of two middle sorted values for even n. Outliers affect mean more strongly than median; standard deviation measures spread in original units.|mean=Σxi/n; population SD=√[Σ(xi-mean)²/n]|Data 1,2,2,9: mean=14/4=3.5, median=(2+2)/2=2, mode=2.|Skewed values? Median often represents a typical value better than mean.|Computing median before sorting or confusing sample n-1 with population n denominator.

PS|Conditional expectation and variance|Within a condition, average using the conditional distribution.|The law of total expectation averages group means. Total variance separates within-group spread and between-group mean variation.|E[X]=E[E[X given Y]]; Var(X)=E[Var(X given Y)]+Var(E[X given Y])|Two equally likely groups have means 2 and 6: overall mean 4.|Compute conditional distributions first, then conditional moments.|Confusing E[X/Y] with E[X given Y].

PS|Covariance and correlation|Covariance reports co-movement; correlation normalizes it to [-1,1].|Zero covariance rules out only linear association, not nonlinear dependence. Independence with finite second moments implies zero covariance; reverse fails.|Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]; Corr=Cov/(σX σY)|If Y=3X+2 and Var(X)>0, Corr(X,Y)=+1.|Perfect affine relationship with positive slope gives +1 immediately.|Treating zero correlation as proof of independence.

PS|Bernoulli distribution|One trial with success probability p has outcomes zero and one.|This is the building block for binomial counts. Mean and variance can be read from p without enumerating events.|X~Bernoulli(p); E[X]=p; Var(X)=p(1-p)|For success probability .2, variance=.2×.8=.16.|Recognize a 0/1 indicator variable as Bernoulli.|Using the number of trials n for a single Bernoulli.

PS|Binomial distribution|Count successes among n independent identical Bernoulli trials.|The binomial coefficient chooses which trials succeed; all those arrangements have the same probability if p is fixed.|P(X=k)=nCk p^k(1-p)^(n-k); mean=np; variance=np(1-p)|Three fair coin tosses exactly two heads: 3(.5)^3=3/8.|For at least one success use 1-(1-p)^n.|Applying binomial to draws without replacement from a small set.

PS|Discrete uniform and geometric intuition|Uniform means equally likely values; geometric models waiting for first success.|A discrete uniform variable on {1,...,n} has mean (n+1)/2. Geometric waiting is memoryless and is useful as an extra bridge to distributions.|Discrete uniform P(X=k)=1/n; mean=(n+1)/2|Fair die mean=(1+6)/2=3.5.|Use symmetry to find mean of equally spaced endpoints.|Confusing geometric waiting time with number of successes.

PS|Continuous PDF and normalization|A density is not a point probability; area under the curve is probability.|Continuous X has P(X=a)=0. A valid density is nonnegative and integrates to one. Intervals use integrals or CDF differences.|P(a≤X≤b)=∫a^b f(x)dx|If f(x)=2x for 0<x<1, P(X≤.5)=∫0^.5 2x dx=.25.|Check units and total area first.|Saying f(x)>1 is impossible; densities can exceed one.

PS|Continuous uniform distribution|Every equal-length subinterval of the support has equal probability.|The uniform density on [a,b] is 1/(b-a). Its mean is midpoint and variance is width squared divided by twelve.|E[X]=(a+b)/2; Var=(b-a)²/12|For X~U(2,6), P(3<X<5)=2/4=.5.|Compute interval length / support length directly.|Treating endpoints as carrying positive mass.

PS|Exponential distribution|Exponential models the waiting time until a Poisson-process event.|Its memorylessness says future waiting time does not depend on how long you have already waited. λ is a rate, not a mean.|f(x)=λe^(-λx) for x≥0; E[X]=1/λ|With λ=2, P(X>1)=e^(-2).|Survival function exp(-λt) is faster than integration.|Substituting mean instead of rate λ.

PS|Poisson distribution|Poisson describes the count of rare events in a fixed interval.|Its single parameter λ is both mean and variance. It can approximate Binomial(n,p) if n large, p small and np≈λ.|P(X=k)=e^(-λ)λ^k/k!; E[X]=Var(X)=λ|For λ=2, P(X=0)=e^(-2).|At k=0 the formula simplifies to exp(-λ).|Confusing the Poisson count with exponential waiting time.

PS|Normal and standard normal|A normal distribution is a symmetric bell curve determined by mean and variance.|Standardize using Z=(X-μ)/σ; standard normal probabilities are read using CDF Φ. Symmetry gives Φ(-z)=1-Φ(z).|X~N(μ,σ²); Z=(X-μ)/σ|X~N(10,4), value 14 corresponds to z=(14-10)/2=2.|Before table lookup, standardize and use symmetry.|Using variance as if it were standard deviation.

PS|t and chi-squared distributions|The t distribution handles standardized means when variance is estimated; chi-square accumulates squared normals.|t has heavier tails than normal for small degrees of freedom and approaches normal as degrees grow. A sum of k independent squared standard normals is χ²(k).|t=(Xbar-μ)/(s/√n); ΣZi²~χ²(k)|For n=9, mean=11, hypothesized μ=10, s=3: t=(1)/(3/3)=1 with 8 df.|Degrees of freedom for one-sample t is n-1.|Using z when σ is unknown and sample is very small without justification.

PS|Joint continuous and conditional PDF|For two continuous variables, probabilities come from volumes under a joint density.|Find marginal fX(x) by integrating over y, then conditional fY given X(y given x)=fXY(x,y)/fX(x), when fX(x)>0.|fY_given_X(y given x)=fXY(x,y)/fX(x)|If fXY=2 on triangle 0<y<x<1, fX(x)=2x and fY_given_X=1/x for 0<y<x.|Always find integration limits from support diagram.|Integrating over a rectangle when support is triangular.

PS|Law of large numbers and CLT|Sample averages stabilize; the CLT describes their approximate distribution.|For many independent observations with finite variance, standardized sample mean tends to N(0,1). Standard error of mean is σ/√n.|Z≈(Xbar-μ)/(σ/√n)|For σ=10 and n=100, SE=1.|Quadrupling n halves standard error.|Assuming the original data must be normally distributed for CLT approximation.

PS|Sampling distributions and standard error|A statistic changes across repeated samples; its sampling distribution quantifies that uncertainty.|Sample variance often uses n-1 for an unbiased variance estimate. Different estimators have different standard errors.|SE(Xbar)=σ/√n; s²=Σ(xi-Xbar)²/(n-1)|If σ=12 and n=36, SE=2.|Separate population SD σ from sample-mean SE.|Interpreting sample SD and standard error as identical.

PS|Confidence intervals|A confidence interval is produced by a procedure with long-run coverage.|For known σ, a two-sided 95% interval for μ uses ±1.96 standard errors. Unknown σ and small sample generally use t critical values.|CI=Xbar±z*σ/√n (known σ)|Xbar=50, σ=10, n=100: approximate 95% CI=50±1.96= [48.04,51.96].|Margin of error is critical value × SE.|Claiming 95% probability the fixed parameter lies in one computed interval.

PS|Hypothesis testing and p-values|A hypothesis test checks whether data are surprising under a null model.|p-value is the probability, assuming H0, of evidence at least as extreme as observed. Significance α controls Type I error probability.|Reject H0 when p≤α|If p=.03 and α=.05, reject H0; at α=.01, fail to reject.|Decide one-sided vs two-sided before computing a statistic.|Treating p as P(H0 true given data).

PS|z-test and t-test|Tests of a mean scale the observed difference by a standard error.|Use z when population variance is known or large-sample approximation applies; for normal small samples with unknown σ, use t with df=n-1.|z=(Xbar-μ0)/(σ/√n); t=(Xbar-μ0)/(s/√n)|Xbar=12, μ0=10, σ=4, n=16: z=(2)/(1)=2.|Check assumptions and standard error before comparing to critical value.|Using sample variance as a denominator without square root.

PS|Chi-squared tests|Chi-squared statistics compare observed categorical counts with expected counts.|For goodness-of-fit, Σ(O-E)²/E measures deviation. For independence, expected cell count=row total×column total/grand total.|χ²=Σ(O-E)²/E|Observed (30,20), expected (25,25): χ²=25/25+25/25=2.|Compute expected counts first and ensure categories partition observations.|Feeding raw probabilities instead of expected counts into formula.

LA|Vectors, dot products and norms|Vectors encode direction and magnitude; dot product measures alignment.|Dot product is zero for perpendicular vectors. Norm is square root of self-dot-product. The geometric angle is derived from normalized dot product.|a·b=Σaibi; NORMaNORM=√(a·a)|a=(3,4): NORMaNORM=5; (1,0)·(0,1)=0.|Use dot product zero to test orthogonality quickly.|Confusing dot product scalar with cross product vector.

LA|Vector spaces and subspaces|A vector space is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a subspace inherits these rules.|Test that zero vector belongs and that any linear combination of vectors in the proposed set stays inside. Span of vectors is always a subspace.|a u+b v∈W for all u,v∈W|W={(x,y):x+y=0} is a subspace because sums and scalar multiples keep x+y=0.|For a homogeneous linear constraint Ax=0, solution set is always a subspace.|Assuming affine line x+y=1 is a subspace (it misses zero).

LA|Span, basis and dimension|Span is all linear combinations; a basis is a smallest independent spanning set.|Dimension counts basis vectors. Two linearly independent vectors in R² span the whole plane. An m×n matrix maps Rn to Rm.|dim(span)=number of basis vectors|Vectors (1,0),(0,1) form a basis of R²; dimension 2.|For full rank square matrices, columns form a basis.|Counting nonzero vectors instead of independent ones.

LA|Linear dependence and independence|Dependence means one vector can be built from others.|Columns are independent iff Ax=0 has only the trivial solution. More vectors than ambient dimension guarantee dependence.|independent ⇔ null(A)={0}|(1,2) and (2,4) are dependent because second=2×first.|With >n vectors in Rn, dependence is automatic.|Assuming orthogonality is required for independence.

LA|Matrix operations and transpose|Matrices represent linear transformations and systems of equations.|Matrix multiplication composes transformations and is generally not commutative. Transpose swaps rows and columns; (AB)ᵀ=BᵀAᵀ.|(AB)ij=Σk Aik Bkj; (AB)ᵀ=BᵀAᵀ|A is 2×3, B is 3×4, then AB is 2×4.|Check inner dimensions before multiplication.|Assuming AB=BA or swapping transpose order incorrectly.

LA|Determinants and invertibility|Determinant measures oriented volume scaling; zero means collapse to a lower dimension.|For square A, det(A)≠0 iff A is invertible iff full rank. Row swap changes sign; scaling row scales det.|det([[a,b],[c,d]])=ad-bc|det([[2,1],[3,4]])=8-3=5.|Triangular determinant is product of diagonal entries.|Using det for nonsquare matrices.

LA|Rank and nullity|Rank counts independent columns; nullity counts free input directions killed by A.|Row reduction reveals pivots, thus rank. For A with n columns, rank+nullity=n regardless of the number of rows.|rank(A)+nullity(A)=n columns|For 3 columns and rank 2, nullity=1.|Count columns, not rows, in rank-nullity.|Claiming nullity is m-rank for m×n A.

LA|Gaussian elimination and RREF|Row operations simplify a linear system without changing its solutions.|Swap rows, scale a nonzero row, or add multiples of rows. Pivots reveal unique, infinitely many, or inconsistent systems.|Inconsistent row: [0 ... 0 ; c], c≠0|x+y=3 and x-y=1; add equations: 2x=4 -> x=2,y=1.|Augmented matrix is fastest for small systems.|Dividing by zero during pivoting.

LA|Systems of equations and solution types|A system has a unique solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions.|Compare rank(A) and rank([A;b]). Equal ranks mean consistent; if rank(A)=number of variables the solution is unique.|consistent iff rank(A)=rank([A;b])|x+y=2 and 2x+2y=5 are inconsistent because doubled first gives 4 not 5.|Compare dependent equations before full elimination.|Assuming a square system is automatically solvable.

LA|Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|An eigenvector keeps its direction under a linear transformation.|Solve det(A-λI)=0 for eigenvalues, then (A-λI)v=0 for nonzero v. Trace is sum and determinant product of eigenvalues counting multiplicity.|Av=λv; det(A-λI)=0|For diag(2,3), eigenvalues are 2 and 3 with coordinate axes eigenvectors.|Triangular matrix eigenvalues are diagonal entries.|Allowing the zero vector as an eigenvector.

LA|Diagonalization and spectral intuition|Some transformations become simple scaling in an eigenvector basis.|If A has n independent eigenvectors, A=PDP⁻¹. Symmetric real matrices admit orthogonal diagonalization. Repeated eigenvalues need not supply enough eigenvectors.|A=PDP⁻¹|For diag(2,3), A²=diag(4,9) directly.|Distinct eigenvalues guarantee diagonalizability.|Believing every square matrix is diagonalizable.

LA|Orthogonal matrices and projections|Orthogonal matrices preserve inner products and lengths; projections keep only a component.|QᵀQ=I implies Q⁻¹=Qᵀ. Orthogonal projection onto span(u) uses uuᵀ/(uᵀu). Projection matrices are symmetric idempotent.|P=uuᵀ/(uᵀu); P²=P|Project (3,4) onto x-axis: (3,0).|Orthogonal Q has eigenvalues with magnitude 1 and determinant ±1.|Confusing a projection (usually noninvertible) with a rotation.

LA|Idempotent and partitioned matrices|Idempotence means applying a transformation twice does nothing new; block partitions simplify structured calculations.|A matrix P with P²=P has eigenvalues only 0 or 1. Partitioned matrix multiplication follows ordinary conformable block multiplication.|P²=P ⇒ λ²=λ ⇒ λ∈{0,1}|P=diag(1,0) satisfies P²=P and has rank 1.|Trace of an idempotent matrix equals its rank.|Assuming every idempotent matrix is symmetric.

LA|Quadratic forms and definiteness|A quadratic form xᵀAx describes curvature and energy.|For symmetric A, positive definite means xᵀAx>0 for every nonzero x, equivalent to all eigenvalues positive. Cross terms come from off-diagonal coefficients.|q(x)=xᵀAx|A=diag(2,3) gives q=2x₁²+3x₂²>0 for x≠0.|For symmetric 2×2, a11>0 and determinant>0 imply positive definite.|Ignoring symmetry when using eigenvalue definiteness rules.

LA|LU decomposition|LU factors a matrix into lower- and upper-triangular factors for repeated solves.|Gaussian elimination produces U and stores elimination multipliers in L; pivoting may require PA=LU.|A=LU (when no pivoting needed)|For [[2,1],[4,3]], L=[[1,0],[2,1]], U=[[2,1],[0,1]].|Use forward substitution then backward substitution to solve Ax=b.|Assuming LU always exists without row permutations.

LA|Singular value decomposition|SVD decomposes any real matrix into input rotation, scaling, and output rotation.|A=UΣVᵀ where U,V are orthogonal and singular values are nonnegative. Number of nonzero singular values equals rank; squares relate to eigenvalues of AᵀA.|A=UΣVᵀ; σi=√eigenvalue_i(AᵀA)|For A=diag(3,2), singular values are 3 and 2.|For a diagonal nonnegative matrix, singular values are its diagonal values.|Confusing singular values with possibly negative eigenvalues.

LA|Least squares and pseudoinverse|When Ax=b has no exact solution, least squares finds the closest fit.|Minimize NORMAx-bNORM². If columns of A are independent, normal equations yield x=(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb; pseudoinverse handles general rank.|AᵀAx=Aᵀb|Fit y=c to observations 2,4,6: best constant c=4.|Mean minimizes total squared deviations.|Inverting AᵀA blindly when A is rank deficient.

CA|Functions, domains and graphs|A function maps each allowed input to exactly one output.|Domain restrictions come from division by zero, even roots of negatives, and logarithms of nonpositive values. Graph transformations let you interpret equations.|Domain of ln x is x>0|f(x)=1/(x-2) has every real x except 2 in its domain.|Check denominator, square roots, logs before algebra.|Ignoring the domain while cancelling factors.

CA|Limits and one-sided limits|A limit describes a value approached, regardless of whether the function is defined there.|A two-sided limit exists only if left and right limits agree. Factorization and rationalization resolve many 0/0 forms.|lim(x→a) f(x)=L requires both one-sided limits equal L|lim(x→2)(x²-4)/(x-2)=lim(x+2)=4.|Factor or rationalize before using advanced rules.|Substituting into 0/0 and calling the answer zero.

CA|Continuity|A function is continuous at a if its value matches the limit from both sides.|Continuity requires f(a) defined, limit exists, and the two are equal. Differentiability implies continuity but not conversely.|lim(x→a)f(x)=f(a)|f(x)=abs(x) is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there.|For piecewise functions test matching left/right values.|Assuming continuity guarantees smooth derivatives.

CA|Derivatives and rules|Derivative is the instantaneous rate of change, or slope of the tangent line.|Power, product, quotient and chain rules let you differentiate composites. Chain rule multiplies outside derivative by inside derivative.|d(x^n)/dx=nx^(n-1); (f∘g)'=f'(g)g'|d[(3x+1)²]/dx=2(3x+1)×3=6(3x+1).|For a nested function work outside in.|Forgetting the derivative of the inner function.

CA|Mean value theorem and monotonicity|Derivative sign indicates increasing or decreasing behaviour.|For continuous f on [a,b] differentiable inside, some c has f'(c)=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a). A positive derivative across interval implies increasing.|f'(c)=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a)|For f=x² on [1,3], secant slope=4; f'(c)=2c=4 -> c=2.|Use monotonicity to bound values without evaluating every point.|Applying mean value theorem at a discontinuity.

CA|Taylor and Maclaurin series|Taylor polynomials approximate a smooth function near a chosen point using derivatives.|Maclaurin is Taylor around zero. Terms beyond first order capture curvature. Remainder matters away from expansion point.|f(x)≈f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+f''(a)(x-a)²/2|e^x≈1+x+x²/2 near 0; for x=.1, ≈1.105.|Remember standard expansions of e^x, sin x, cos x, ln(1+x).|Assuming a truncated series is exact for large x.

CA|Stationary points and first-derivative test|A stationary point has derivative zero; extrema require a sign change or boundary reasoning.|Local minimum often changes derivative from negative to positive; local maximum from positive to negative. Also check points where derivative does not exist.|f'(x*)=0 is a candidate, not a conclusion|f(x)=x³ has f'(0)=0 but no max/min at 0.|Construct a derivative sign table.|Declaring every zero derivative a local extremum.

CA|Second-derivative test and curvature|Second derivative captures curvature near a stationary point.|At f'(x*)=0, positive f'' means local minimum, negative means maximum. Zero second derivative is inconclusive.|f''(x*)>0 -> local min if f'(x*)=0|f=x²: f'(0)=0 and f''(0)=2>0, so min at 0.|One second derivative can avoid a long sign table.|Using test when f''=0 as if it were decisive.

CA|Global optimization and endpoints|A global optimum is best over the entire feasible domain.|On a closed bounded interval for a continuous function, compare candidate critical values and both endpoints. Constraints can move the optimum to a boundary.|Compare f(a), f(b), and f(x*) for feasible critical points|On [0,3], f=(x-2)² has min 0 at x=2; max 4 at x=0.|Always inspect endpoints after derivative tests.|Reporting an out-of-range stationary point.

CA|Gradient descent in one dimension|Optimization can iteratively move downhill using local slope.|Update x by subtracting learning-rate times gradient. Too-large learning rates overshoot or diverge; too-small rates crawl.|x(next)=x-now - η f'(x-now)|f=x², x0=4, η=.25 -> x1=4-.25(8)=2.|For quadratic ax², stable step sizes depend on curvature.|Assuming a higher learning rate is always faster.

PDSA|Python types, variables and expressions|Python evaluates expressions using types, precedence and operator semantics.|Lists are mutable, tuples immutable, dictionaries map keys to values, sets store unique values. Division / produces float; // is floor division, even for negatives.|-3//2=-2; -3%2=1|7//2=3 whereas 7/2=3.5.|For code-output questions check operator order and negative operands.|Assuming // truncates toward zero.

PDSA|Conditionals, loops and ranges|Control flow executes branches and repetitions based on conditions.|range(start,stop,step) excludes stop. Break exits a loop and continue skips to next iteration. for-else runs else only without break.|range(1,6,2) -> 1,3,5|sum(range(1,5))=1+2+3+4=10.|Make a tiny trace table for 2-3 iterations.|Including stop in range.

PDSA|Functions, recursion and scope|Functions reuse logic; recursion solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances.|Every terminating recursion needs a base case and progress toward it. Local variables differ from outer scope. Count calls or stack frames in recursive tracing.|T(n)=T(n-1)+O(1) for a simple chain|factorial(4)=4×3×2×1=24 via recursive calls.|Draw a call tree for branch recursion, a chain for single recursion.|Forgetting base case or confusing print with return.

PDSA|Lists, slicing and comprehension|A list is an indexed mutable sequence; slicing creates selected elements.|Slice [start:stop:step] excludes stop and supports negative indices. List comprehension loops with optional filtering. Nested list references can alias.|a[-1] is last element; a[1:4] selects indices 1,2,3|a=[0,1,2,3,4]; a[::-1]=[4,3,2,1,0].|Use index labels to decode a slice.|Assuming assigning b=a copies all nested contents.

PDSA|Dictionaries, sets and hashing|Hash maps provide key-based access; sets keep unique elements.|Average-case hash table lookup is O(1) under good hashing; pathological collisions can make operations slower. Dictionary keys must be hashable.|Average lookup: O(1)|len(set([1,1,2,3]))=3.|When only membership matters, set beats repeated list scans.|Claiming worst-case hash lookup must be O(1).

PDSA|Time complexity and asymptotic notation|Big-O expresses growth rather than exact seconds.|Drop constants and lower-order terms for asymptotic upper bounds. Nested independent loops multiply; consecutive loops add; halving loops are logarithmic.|O(n²+n)=O(n²); binary halving O(log n)|Loop i=0..n-1, inner j=0..n-1: n² operations.|Count how the problem size changes per iteration.|Believing every nested loop is O(n²), even triangular or halving loops.

PDSA|Space complexity and recursion stack|Memory used by input, auxiliary structures and call stack can dominate algorithms.|Separate total space from extra (auxiliary) space. A recursion of depth n usually needs O(n) frames even if each frame stores O(1).|Recursion depth n -> O(n) stack|Recursive factorial uses n frames: O(n) call stack.|Always count hidden recursion stack.|Calling recursion O(1) space because no array was allocated.

PDSA|Arrays versus linked lists|Arrays support indexing; linked lists support pointer-based local insertion.|Array indexing is O(1), but insertion at front usually shifts elements O(n). Singly linked list insertion with known predecessor is O(1), but traversal is O(n).|Array access O(1); linked-list indexed access O(n)|To reach fifth linked-list node from head traverse 4 next pointers.|Ask whether node reference is already available.|Assuming locating insertion point in linked list is O(1).

PDSA|Stacks and applications|Stack is last-in-first-out, like a pile of plates.|Push, pop and peek occur at the top. Stacks support recursion, expression evaluation and balanced-parentheses matching.|LIFO; push/pop O(1) normally|Push 1, push 2, pop -> 2; remaining top is 1.|Trace with a vertical list and top marker.|Removing from the bottom instead of top.

PDSA|Queues and circular queues|Queue is first-in-first-out, like a waiting line.|Enqueue at rear, dequeue at front.
